doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Substituting in Broadway shows
summary: Jimmy subbed in Broadway pits without rehearsal, learning to read and stay on the rhythm.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: I mean it’s a long process. But you’ve got a lot of — What was it like working with, you did some Broadway shows and all that.

Yeah, that was another great experience, a broadening experience you know, to be called in as a sub you see. So every time I did one, there was no rehearsal. And that’s where the challenge was. And as you say, state and maintain a competence. Because you had no idea what’s going on. Every now and then maybe you had an opportunity to go in maybe to a matinee and sit in the pit, and just see what’s going on. But most of the time, like phew. You’d get there an hour ahead of time and then the conductor comes over, oh, you’re the substitute, so-and-so. So it would work out.
Plus you have to — it’s not like a jazz gig where you’re being able to improvise a lot. Reading those notes.

No. Everything has to be right there. Because you’re dealing with the performance on the stage, singing-wise and stuff like that and everything, and dancing and all that bit, so you definitely learn quickly how not to mess with the rhythm by coming in wrong. It’s kind of faux pas. It’s best you leave it out, because the next phrase, you know the next letter or whatever, rather than try to stick it though, you’ll be sticking out there like a sore thumb. Everybody’d be dancing and they’ll turn around. What the hell’s going on? But that was really, like I say, a very good experience. It taught me a lot, and also in terms of how to share that — that process — share that with, in terms of education, to students. Like dealing with the attitudes and emotions of everybody concerned.
